reference.title: if + past, would / wouldn't + infinitive
rows: If she didn't have a dog,
if there were sharks in the sea?
Would you go for a swim
we could stop at places on the way.

reference.text: We use if + past to talk about an imaginary or hypothetical future situation and would / wouldn't + infinitive to talk about the consequence. We also use would without an if-clause: I'd never have a cat as a pet. would / wouldn't is the same for all persons: 'd = would, wouldn't = would not.

reference.title: Word order
reference.text: The if-clause can come first or second. If it comes first, we usually put a comma before the next clause: If I had more time, I'd do more exercise. / I'd do more exercise if I had more time.

reference.title: could
reference.text: We can also use could + infinitive instead of would + infinitive: If we went by car, we could stop at places on the way.

reference.title: be in second conditionals
reference.text: With be we can use were instead of was after I / he / she / it: If Jack was / were here, he'd know what to do. Use were (not was) in If I were you… – we often use it for advice: If I were you, I wouldn't take that job.

reference.title: First or second conditional?
rows: If I don't have to work tomorrow, I'll help you. (Maybe I will help you.)
If I didn't have to work tomorrow, I'd help you. (I have to work, so I can't help you.)

reference.wrong: If I would have more money, I would buy a car.
reference.right: If I had more money, I would buy a car.
reference.why: After if we use the past, not would.
